_comment: Static scoreboard metadata. Display order below is the on-page card order (deliberately shuffled). `rows` come from bench_refresh/benchmarks.json via build.py. `updated` is set by build.py from the fetch date.

aa.example: An agentic workflow task: given a set of tools, research three vendors, compare pricing, and draft a recommendation memo. Scored on the share of objectives actually completed — a single safety violation zeroes the task.
aa.name: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
aa.note: Artificial Analysis revised this index's methodology several times in September 2026 (v4.1.1 → v4.3.2); scores are not comparable across versions.
aa.what: One number summarizing a model across four equally weighted pillars — agentic tasks, coding, scientific reasoning, and general knowledge — from evaluations run independently by Artificial Analysis. The 2026 scale was recalibrated so today's frontier lands around 45–55, leaving headroom above.

ab.example: Close a €120k Salesforce deal: disambiguate 'Meridian Corp' from lookalike accounts, convert currency at the latest FX rate, check for open critical escalations, route the win email per policy — and make sure the wrong teams were NOT emailed.
ab.name: AutomationBench
ab.note: Scores from the 600-task public set; the official board runs a private set. Strict grading: every assertion must pass.
ab.what: Zapier's test of whether agents can complete realistic multi-step business workflows — sales, marketing, ops, support, finance, HR — by discovering REST APIs across dozens of simulated SaaS environments while following business rules. Graded on whether the right data ended up in the right systems.

fc.example: A real open-source PR like 'ellipsis on long emails,' graded against 14 reviewer criteria. Peek at the upstream diff to shortcut the answer and the run scores zero.
fc.name: FrontierCode 1.1
fc.note: Main track (100 private tasks). The source board mixes independent runs with vendor-reported ones.
fc.what: Cognition's test of whether coding agents write pull requests good enough that real open-source maintainers would merge them — graded on quality, scope discipline, and style, not just whether the tests pass. All 100 Main-track tasks are private.

hle.example: A biology stumper like the hummingbird sesamoid-bone question: 'How many paired tendons are supported by this sesamoid bone? Answer with a number.' Graduate-exam difficulty in every field.
hle.name: Humanity's Last Exam
hle.note: Official Scale AI board, full 2,500-question set. Ranks use statistical-significance ties, so several models share a rank. Third-party mirrors use a smaller text-only subset and are not comparable.
hle.what: 2,500 extremely hard questions written by around a thousand domain experts across 100+ subjects — 41% math — each of which had to stump every frontier model at launch and survive two rounds of expert review. Designed as the last academic exam before AI passes expert humans.

tb.example: Set up an Nginx reverse proxy with TLS for the app in /srv/app, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and verify with curl that https://localhost returns 200. The agent starts from a bare container and a goal.
tb.name: Terminal-Bench 4.0
tb.note: Official leaderboard rows are model×effort runs; shown is each model's best run. Resolution rate, with 95% confidence intervals on the source.
tb.what: The model works as an autonomous agent inside a real Linux terminal — shell, filesystem, package managers, network — completing end-to-end jobs like configuring servers or running data pipelines. An automated checker grades the final system state.

tbs.example: Given TESS space-telescope light-curve data, detect and vet exoplanet transit candidates and produce a verifiable analysis — astronomy done end-to-end from a terminal.
tbs.name: Terminal-Bench Science 0.1
tbs.note: Resolution rate over 70 tasks × 3 trials; 95% confidence intervals on the source. The board updates as new evals land.
tbs.what: Stanford and the Laude Institute's test of AI agents doing real scientific research in a Linux terminal — 70 expert-curated, objectively verifiable workflows across the life, physical, earth, mathematical, and engineering sciences.
